title: Grant me this
hook: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai: grant that I never turn from good deeds and fear no foe (Dasam, Chandi Charitar)

segments.voice: Yesterday, your line: tell the friend. Did you send one honest message? It closes a week that held the hem, rested in His refuge, heard many names for one Lord, watched the light pass on, and gave thanks for unseen help. Today, a short request that Sikhs sing standing tall. Day six hundred seventy-two.
screen: `HOLDING THE HEM · IN HIS REFUGE · MANY NAMES · THE LIGHT PASSES ON · YOU MADE ME WORTHY · TELL THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: When people ask for something big, it's often comfort: let the test go well, let the scan be clear, let the money come through. Fair enough. This verse asks for something else: the strength not to quit doing what's right, even when it costs. Not an easy road. A steady spine. Not to be spared trouble, but to stay good inside it. Sikhs hold it as the Tenth Guru's, and Sikh children learn to sing it. Today: grant me this.
screen: `ASKING FOR COMFORT.` → `THIS ONE ASKS FOR A SPINE.` → `A VERSE CHILDREN LEARN TO SING.`

segments.voice: The verse comes near the end of Chandi Charitar, a long poem in the Dasam Granth. Its first words: deh sivaa bar mohi ihai. In paraphrase: grant me this boon, that I never turn away from good deeds. That when I go to face the enemy, I'm not afraid, and I win with resolve. That I teach my own mind this lesson: to sing Your praises. And when my life's end comes, let me die fighting in the field. Start with the first ask: subh karman te kabhoon na taro. Never turn back from good deeds. That's the center of it. Courage in battle comes after it, and can be read as serving it. Then notice who's being taught: my own mind. The verse doesn't ask God to change other people. It asks for a mind that keeps choosing good. Who is Sivaa, the one being asked? Sikhs read it in different ways. Some hear Sivaa as a name for God's own power, the Timeless One, who is addressed by many names in the Dasam Granth. Others read it within the setting of the poem, which tells of the goddess Chandi's battles, and hear the verse as the poet's request at its close. Scholars discuss it, and the verse is loved either way. Whichever reading, what stays is the shape of the request. It's a prayer for character, not circumstances. The Khalsa ideal of the saint-soldier lives in those four lines: someone gentle enough to sing God's praise, and steady enough never to walk away from what's right.
screen: `DEH SIVAA: GRANT ME THIS.` · `NEVER TURN FROM GOOD DEEDS.` · `TEACH MY OWN MIND.` · `CHARACTER, NOT CIRCUMSTANCES.` · then, large: `NEVER TURN FROM GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: commit to one good deed. Sit up straight. Think of one good thing you've been meaning to do and keep putting off: a visit, an apology, a donation, standing up for someone. Picture the moment you'd want to back out, and picture yourself not backing out. Choose it, quietly. If you pray, you can say the verse's first words, deh sivaa bar mohi ihai, or say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Grant me this. The Tenth Guru's verse, deh sivaa bar mohi ihai: may I never turn from good deeds, never fear when I face the enemy, and teach my own mind to sing Your praise.
Your line: never turn from good. Today, do the one good deed you chose, even if the moment to back out comes. Day six hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing deh sivaa bar mohi ihai at gatherings, in schools and in kirtan, often standing, as a prayer for steadiness in doing good.

what it means: it asks first for a mind that never turns from good; courage serves that.

what a scholar hears: the savaiya comes near the close of Chandi Charitar in the Dasam Granth, whose authorship scholars still discuss; the address 'Sivaa' is read by some as God's power and by others within the poem's Chandi narrative.
